topic: Whether expectancy and open-label placebo effects can be delivered digitally through a phone rather than requiring a mailed inert pill.
metadata_note: The research packet misattributes PMC5918690 to Blease, Colloca, and Kaptchuk. Retrieved metadata identifies that article as Colloca and Howick (2018). The Blease, Colloca, and Kaptchuk article is a different 2016 Bioethics publication.

publications.title: Open-label placebo treatment in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial
publications.finding: In a three-week randomized trial, open-label placebo added to treatment as usual was associated with larger reductions in self-reported chronic low-back-pain intensity and back-related disability than treatment as usual alone. The trial randomized 97 adults; 83 completed analysis. Its authors note that outcomes were subjective, the sample was small, and duration was too short for long-term clinical recommendations.

publications.title: Effects of open-label placebos across populations and outcomes: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
publications.finding: Across 60 randomized trials and 63 comparisons involving 4,554 participants, open-label placebos showed a small pooled overall effect. Effects were statistically significant for self-reported outcomes (SMD 0.39) but not for objective outcomes (SMD 0.09; 95% CI −0.12 to 0.29).

publications.title: Induction of Efficacy Expectancies in an Ambulatory Smartphone-Based Digital Placebo Mental Health Intervention: Randomized Controlled Trial
publications.finding: A 20-day inert smartphone intervention in 132 healthy participants manipulated and measured credibility and efficacy expectancy through instructions and feedback. The reported endpoint was expectancy/credibility, not demonstrated symptom improvement in mood, stress, pain, or a clinical condition.

publications.title: Placebos Without Deception: Outcomes, Mechanisms, and Ethics
publications.finding: A review of open-label and dose-extending placebo research and ethics. It describes candidate mechanisms and ethical questions, rather than establishing a singular causal mechanism or proving that contextual factors are irrelevant.

publications.title: Are open-Label Placebos Ethical? Informed Consent and Ethical Equivocations
publications.finding: An ethical analysis of transparently disclosed placebo studies. It argues that open-label placebo disclosures may still contain equivocation about how placebos work and therefore should not be framed as showing that expectation, therapeutic framing, or context are unnecessary.

relationships.evidence: Supports short-term, patient-reported pain and disability improvement when OLP was added to treatment as usual; it does not establish disease modification or durable objective physiological change.
Supports a small OLP effect overall and for self-reported outcomes; objective outcomes were not statistically significant in the pooled analysis.
Defines OLP as transparent administration of a placebo without pharmacologically active ingredients and describes suggestive rationales as a relevant, unresolved component.
A phone intervention can deliver expectancy-oriented instructions and feedback, but this study measured expectancy rather than clinical symptom benefit or equivalence to a physical OLP regimen.
Reviews open-label placebo mechanisms and ethics; it should not be used to claim that conscious expectations, learned associations, framing, or therapeutic context do not matter.
Analyzes whether open-label disclosures can contain ethical equivocation about placebo mechanisms.

The reviewed public page supports marketing of placebo-and-cognitive-restructuring protocols and depictions of OLP gummies, but not ingredient-level inertness or mailing/fulfillment.

claims.production_safe_claim: Open-label placebo interventions have shown small improvements in self-reported symptoms; evidence for objective physiologic or behavioral changes remains inconclusive.

In a 2016 randomized trial, Carvalho and colleagues found that three weeks of open-label placebo plus treatment as usual was associated with larger reductions in self-reported chronic low-back-pain intensity and disability than treatment as usual alone.

Open-label placebo trials disclose that the pill has no active ingredient; conscious belief in pill chemistry is not required, although expectancy, conditioning, adherence, and treatment context may still contribute.
Copables markets 14-day self-guided protocols that it says use placebos and cognitive restructuring; its site depicts and labels products as OLP gummies.

A digital intervention could deliver some contextual components of a placebo protocol—such as prompts, explanations, and expectancy cues—but whether it can reproduce the effects of an open-label placebo pill is untested.

Ted J. Kaptchuk is Professor Emeritus at Harvard Medical School, a Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center research-faculty member, and is associated with the Program in Placebo Studies & Therapeutic Encounter.
